newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Chamorro tries to calm election tension in Nicaragua.
newsitem.headline: Chamorro tries to calm election tension in Nicaragua.

text.p: Nicaraguan President Violeta Chamorro on Wednesday saught to defuse tensions caused by the Sandinistas' refusal to accept voting results giving rightist Arnoldo Aleman victory in Sunday's presidential election.

"I ask (Nicaraguans) to maintain their calm and civility as they await the final results, which should be given by the Supreme Electoral Council as soon as possible," Chamorro said in a radio address to the nation.

With 81.53 percent of the ballots counted, preliminary official results showed Aleman with 48.85 percent, well ahead of former Sandinista president Daniel Ortega, who got 38.51 percent. This puts Aleman easily above the 45 percent threshold needed to avoid a runoff.

Nicaragua's most powerful business group asked Nicaraguans to accept Aleman's victory. "The Superior Council of Private Enterprise ... demands respect for the results ... and that Arnoldo Aleman ... be declared president," it said in a statement.

Tensions soared after the left-wing Sandinistas and eight smaller parties refused to accept the results and demanded a review of Sunday's vote, which Ortega charged was riddled with "serious irregularities."

The Sandinistas said they will accept the results once their local observers at each polling station approve them. With anger and disappointment growing among the militant Sandinista rank-and-file, party leaders said they were taking pains to ensure Ortega's protests did not stir violence.

The bitter presidential race reflected the left-right ideological divide that has torn Nicaragua apart, pitting its former Marxist Sandinista rulers against a right-wing populist linked to former supporters of dictator Anastasio Somoza, who was ousted in the 1979 Sandinista revolution.

Amid the rising tensions and anger, Managua's conservative Cardinal Miguel Obando y Bravo indirectly called on Ortega and the smaller parties to accept the election results. "Politics is like a football game. You have to know how to lose," Obando y Bravo told a news conference.
International observers said the election was fair, despite some delays and disorganization.
Nicaraguan election authorities said they will review the vote count once the preliminary count is finished.
Aleman, the portly former mayor of Managua dubbed the "Fatman," caused rapture among his followers by keeping the Sandinistas, who ruled from 1979 to 1990, out of power.

Besides the presidency, Aleman's Liberal Alliance looked set to win the lion's share of seats in the National Assembly -- though perhaps not a majority -- and a clutch of town halls across the country, including the capital Managua.
